spans.assertion: the analysis used data covering over 300,000 player-referee-match observations

spans.note: restates research question: whether referees exhibit skin-tone bias

spans.assertion: found referees give more red cards to dark skin-toned players, odds ratio 1.179, CI [0.952, 1.405]
found referees give fewer yellow cards to dark skin-toned players, odds ratio 0.958, CI [0.921, 0.994]

spans.note: caveat that results should be taken cautiously due to possible confounders

spans.assertion: used an identification strategy exploiting variation across different referees officiating the same player

spans.note: restates research question 2: whether referee-country implicit/explicit prejudice affects skin-tone bias

spans.assertion: found that a referee's country's implicit or explicit skin-tone prejudice does not affect that referee's skin-tone bias

spans.note: blank lines and 'One Sentence Summary' heading

spans.assertion: found a small amount of referee bias due to skin tone in red cards
found no bias due to skin tone in yellow cards

spans.note: notes the identification strategy is poor, lacks exogenous variation, and results are likely confounded by unobservables such as playing style

spans.assertion: with a good identification strategy, shows no relationship between referee-country implicit/explicit skin-tone prejudice and red cards received by dark skin-toned players

spans.assertion: changed the unit of observation from a player-referee dyad to a player-referee-game observation, expanding the number of rows to equal the number of games played
added squared terms of age, height, and weight as additional control variables
created an average rater value by taking a simple average of the two skin-tone ratings
created standardized (mean 0, sd 1) country-level mean IAT and EXP prejudice scores
did not exclude any observations from the data
for 4 dyad observations with 1 game but 2 recorded yellow cards, recoded the yellow card count to 1 and left redcards/yellowred variables at 0
judged this recoding to be a trivial change given it affects a small fraction of cards
specified model 1 (eq. 1), regressing card outcomes (yellow, hard red, any red) on skin-tone rating, a categorical variable from 1 (very light) to 5 (very dark)
model 1 includes player-characteristic controls: height, height-squared, weight, weight-squared, age, age-squared
model 1 includes referee, league-country, club, and player-position fixed effects
the logistic and non-linear regressions for question 1 use the same controls as the linear model
specified model 2 (eq. 2), regressing outcomes on the referee-country's implicit or explicit prejudice score with a player fixed effect
estimated equation 2 separately for light-skinned players (rating 1-2) and dark-skinned players (rating 3-5)
interprets the difference between the light- and dark-skinned player estimates as showing the relationship between referee-country skin-tone prejudice and cards received by dark-toned players
the tables report results as the change in probability of receiving the indicated card
defines 'red cards' as straight red cards
defines 'any red cards' as straight red cards plus double yellow-red cards
found Tables 1-3 show a small positive effect of dark skin on (hard) red cards

spans.note: notes this effect comes from poorly identified variation and likely excludes many confounding variables

spans.assertion: found Tables 4-6 show similar (small positive) results for any red card
found Tables 7-9 show a small negative effect of dark skin on yellow cards

spans.note: notes the yellow-card effect is also poorly identified and likely excludes many confounding variables

spans.assertion: found Tables 10-12 show no systematic difference in skin-tone bias between referees from high- vs. low-prejudice countries

found a one-point skin-tone increase associated with a 0.000203 (SE 0.000111) increase in probability of a hard red card off a base of 0.00430 (a 4.72% relative increase); 95% CI [-0.000019, 0.000425]
found a one-point skin-tone increase associated with a 0.000340 (SE 0.000152) increase in probability of any red card off a base of 0.00430 (a 4.20% relative increase); 95% CI [0.000036, 0.000644]
found a one-point skin-tone increase associated with a 0.000827 (SE 0.000551) decrease in probability of a yellow card off a base of 0.00430 (a 0.63% relative decrease); 95% CI [-0.000275, 0.001929]
found the question-2a (implicit prejudice) effect size on hard red cards is 0.000554 (p=0.313); 95% CI [-0.001716, 0.002814]
found the question-2a (implicit prejudice) effect size on any red card is 0.000252 (p=0.436); 95% CI [-0.002854, 0.003358]
found the question-2a (implicit prejudice) effect size on yellow cards is -0.003798 (p=0.25); 95% CI [-0.015062, 0.007469]
found the question-2b (explicit prejudice) effect size on hard red cards is 0.001249 (p=0.115); 95% CI [-0.000835, 0.003333]
found the question-2b (explicit prejudice) effect size on any red card is 0.001444 (p=0.155); 95% CI [-0.001400, 0.004288]
found the question-2b (explicit prejudice) effect size on yellow cards is -0.005669 (p=0.135); 95% CI [-0.004619, 0.015957]

spans.note: 'Question 1' subheading restating the research question, with blank lines

spans.assertion: Table 1 (linear probability model) found the skin-tone-rating coefficient on red cards ranges 0.000203-0.000328 across 5 specifications, significant except weakest in the fullest specification with referee fixed effects

Table 2 (logistic regression) found the skin-tone-rating coefficient on red cards ranges 0.000159-0.000309 across 4 specifications, mostly significant; no referee-fixed-effects specification is reported for this logistic model
Table 3 (categorical/non-linear model) found increasing positive coefficients for skin-rating categories 2-5 on red cards, strongest and most significant for rating 5
Table 4 (linear probability model) found the skin-tone-rating coefficient on any red card ranges 0.000275-0.000470 across 5 specifications, mostly significant
Table 5 (logistic regression) found the skin-tone-rating coefficient on any red card ranges 0.00026-0.000452 across 4 specifications, significant; no referee-fixed-effects specification is reported
Table 6 (categorical/non-linear model) found skin-rating category 5 has a significant positive coefficient on any red card across all specifications (about 0.0017-0.0023)

Table 7 (linear probability model) found a negative skin-tone-rating coefficient on yellow cards (-0.000827 to -0.002251), significant in reduced specifications but not significant once referee fixed effects are added

Table 8 (logistic regression) found a negative, significant skin-tone-rating coefficient on yellow cards (-0.001008 to -0.002263) across 4 specifications; no referee-fixed-effects specification is reported
Table 9 (categorical/non-linear model) found a mixed pattern for yellow cards: rating 2 positive and significant, ratings 3-5 mostly negative and significant

spans.note: 'Question 2' subheading restating the research question about referee-country prejudice

spans.assertion: Table 10 found that for hard red cards, the dark-minus-light prejudice difference is not statistically significant once player fixed effects are included (IAT p=0.313, EXP p=0.115)

Table 11 found that for yellow cards, the dark-minus-light prejudice difference is highly significant without player fixed effects but not significant once player fixed effects are included (IAT p=0.25, EXP p=0.135)

Table 12 found that for any red card, the dark-minus-light prejudice difference is significant for IAT without player fixed effects (p=0.021) but not significant elsewhere once player fixed effects are included
